tool.name: Vite
tool.tagline: Fast build tool for websites: instant dev server, live updates, optimized builds
tool.description: Vite is the build tool behind most new web projects. While you work, it serves your code to the browser almost instantly and updates the open page as you save; when you're done, it packs everything into small, fast files for users. React, Vue, Svelte and frameworks such as Nuxt, SvelteKit and Astro are built on it, and it has a large ecosystem of plugins.

glossary.def: A build tool for websites: it serves your project on your own computer while you work and packs it into small, fast files for users.
The bundler built into Vite since version 8, written in Rust for speed. It combines your code files for the browser and also does Vite's pre-bundling.
A JavaScript bundler that Vite used for builds before version 8. Its plugin format became a standard that Vite and Rolldown plugins still follow.
A very fast JavaScript converter and bundler, written in Go, that Vite used before version 8 to convert files and pre-bundle packages.
A set of fast JavaScript tools written in Rust that Vite 8 uses to read, convert and shrink (minify) code.
A programming language that turns into fast machine instructions and avoids many memory bugs. Many new JavaScript tools are written in it for speed.
Vite's dev-server step that combines each installed npm package into one browser-ready file the first time it's needed, and keeps the result for next time.
The map of which file imports which, starting from the entry point. Vite uses it to know what to convert, bundle and update.
A module that says it can take a new version of itself while the page runs. When a file changes, Vite updates the nearest one instead of reloading the page.
React's version of hot module replacement: edited components are swapped into the open page while it keeps what's on screen, such as typed text.
HTML-like tags written inside JavaScript, as React uses: <Button label="Hi" />. It must be converted to plain JavaScript before a browser can run it.
A CSS file named *.module.css whose class names are made unique to that file when imported, so two files can use the same class name without clashing.
A popular extended version of CSS, with extras such as variables and nesting. It has to be converted to plain CSS before browsers can use it.
A URL that holds the file itself, starting with data:, instead of pointing to where the file is. It saves a download for very small files.
A script the browser runs alongside the page, on its own, so heavy calculations don't freeze the page. It talks to the page by sending messages.
A short code computed from a file's contents and added to its name, like logo-Bx3k9.svg. It changes only when the contents change.
Leaving code that nothing uses out of the bundle, like shaking a tree so the dead leaves fall.
Cutting an app's bundle into several files, so the browser downloads some code only when it's needed.
One output file of a bundle. A bundler splits an app into chunks so that code which isn't needed yet can be downloaded later.
Extra code that recreates a newer built-in feature for older browsers that don't have it.
A file that links minified, bundled code back to your original files and lines, so error messages and debuggers show your real code.
A service that serves files exactly as they are, with none of your code running on the server. A built Vite app is just such files.
An import of a package by its name, like import x from "react", instead of by a file path like "./x.js".
Universal Module Definition: an old JavaScript file format meant to work everywhere, with CommonJS, older loaders or a plain <script> tag.
A chain of downloads where each file is found only after the previous one arrives, so all their waiting times add up.
Vite's way of building a package for other projects to install, with fixed file names and its dependencies left out, instead of building a website.
In Vite and Rollup, a function in a plugin that the tool calls at a set moment, such as when an import is looked up or a file is loaded, so the plugin can step in.
A module that a plugin makes up in memory instead of reading it from a file. Code imports it like any other module.
Running Vite's dev server inside your own Node server instead of on its own, so your server decides how each request is answered.
Vite's system (since Vite 6) for building and running code for several targets at once, such as the browser and the server, each with its own settings and module graph.
The part of Vite's Environment API that actually runs an environment's modules, in Node or in another JavaScript runtime.
A file such as index.ts that only re-exports many other modules, so they can all be imported from one place.

concepts.name: What Vite is and why it is fast
concepts.summary: Vite runs your project on your own computer while you work, then packs it into small, fast files for real users.
concepts.why: Vite works one way while you develop and another way when it builds for users; knowing that explains most surprises you'll meet.
concepts.body:
In the modules lesson you split a program into files that `import` each other, and met the **bundler**: a tool that combines those files for the browser. A real website may have thousands of files, plus styles, images and packages from npm. Something has to turn all of that into what a browser can load: a **build tool**. **Vite** (French for "fast", said "veet") is the most popular one today.

While you work, Vite runs a **dev server**: a small server program on your own computer that hands your files to your browser. You open an address like `http://localhost:5173` and see your app. Here localhost is the name your computer uses for itself, and 5173 is the **port**: a numbered door the server listens at, so several servers can share one machine.

Older bundlers such as webpack combine the whole app before the dev server can show anything, so starting up and seeing each change get slower as the app grows. Vite skips that step. Modern browsers understand `import` themselves, so Vite hands them your files one at a time, as ES modules, exactly when the page asks for each, converting TypeScript and the like into plain JavaScript on the way. A big app starts about as fast as a small one.

Packages from npm are the exception. Some are made of hundreds of small files, and some use CommonJS, which browsers can't load. So on the first start Vite **pre-bundles** them: it combines each package into one browser-ready file and keeps the result for next time.

When you save a change, Vite updates the open page in place within a fraction of a second, often keeping what you'd typed or clicked. This is **hot module replacement (HMR)**.

When the app is ready for users, `vite build` bundles everything with **Rolldown**, Vite's built-in bundler, into a few files in a `dist/` folder. It also **minifies** them: removes spaces, comments and long names so they download faster but work the same.

Development and the build work differently, so something that works in the dev server can still break after building. Before you **deploy** (put the files on a server where users can reach them), run `vite build`, then `vite preview` to serve the built files on your computer for a final check.

To start a project, run `npm create vite@latest` and pick a **template**, a ready-made starter project: plain JavaScript, or React or Vue (libraries for building pages from reusable pieces), with or without TypeScript. Vite 8 needs Node 20.19+ or 22.12+.
concepts.code:
npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts   # React + TypeScript starter
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev        # start the dev server
#   VITE v8.x  ready in 300 ms
#   ➜  Local:   http://localhost:5173/

npm run build      # bundle and minify everything into dist/
npm run preview    # serve dist/ on http://localhost:4173 to check it
takeaways: While you work, the dev server hands files to the browser one at a time, converting each on request
npm packages are pre-bundled once and kept for next time
`vite build` bundles and minifies everything into dist/ for users
Check with `vite build` + `vite preview` before you deploy
pitfalls: Assuming that because the app works in the dev server, the built app works too; the two paths differ.

quiz.q: Why does Vite's dev server start quickly even for a large app?
options: It keeps the finished bundle on disk from last time
It hands files to the browser one at a time, converting each only when asked
It downloads them from the internet
quiz.explain: Nothing is combined up front: the browser asks for each module and Vite converts it on the spot.

options: Starting the dev server with live updates
Serving the built dist/ files on your computer to check them before deploying
Showing a list of your files
quiz.explain: It serves the output of `vite build` locally, so you test what users will actually get.

concepts.name: Project structure and the CLI
concepts.summary: Learn why index.html is where a Vite app starts, what goes in public/ versus src/, and the dev, build and preview commands.
concepts.why: Vite's folder rules differ from older tools, and knowing them prevents broken file paths.
concepts.body:
Open a fresh Vite project and the first file to notice is `index.html`, sitting at the top of the project folder. It is the app's **entry point**: the file where everything starts. Vite reads it, finds the line `<script type="module" src="/src/main.ts">`, follows that file's imports, then their imports, and so on. This map of which file imports which is the **module graph**.

When you build, Vite writes a new copy of `index.html` into `dist/`, with its script and style links pointing at the finished files. A site with several pages simply has several HTML files.

The usual layout:

- `index.html`: the entry. Paths in it that start with `/src/` are read from the project folder.
- `src/`: your code, plus the images and other files your code imports. Everything here is processed: converted, minified and renamed with a fingerprint of its contents, like `logo-Bx3k9.svg`.
- `public/`: files copied **unchanged** to the top of `dist/` and served at `/`. Use it for files that must keep their exact name, such as `robots.txt` (instructions for search engines) or `favicon.ico` (the little icon on the browser tab). Link to them as `/robots.txt`; never `import` them.
- `vite.config.ts` (optional): Vite's settings.

The commands:

- `vite` (or `vite dev`): start the dev server on port 5173. Add `--open` to open a browser, or `--host` to let other devices on your network, such as your phone, open it too.
- `vite build`: build for users into `dist/`.
- `vite preview`: serve `dist/` on port 4173 to check the build. It's for checking only, not for real users.

In `package.json`, the `dev`, `build` and `preview` scripts usually run these commands, so you type `npm run dev`.

One surprise with TypeScript: Vite only **removes** the type notes so the browser can run the code. It never checks whether they are right. That's why TypeScript starter projects run `tsc -b`, TypeScript's own checker, before `vite build`: if a type is wrong, the build stops.
concepts.code:
my-app/
├── index.html            # entry point (at the top level!)
├── public/
│   └── robots.txt        # copied unchanged -> /robots.txt
├── src/
│   ├── main.ts           # <script type="module" src="/src/main.ts">
│   ├── App.tsx
│   └── assets/logo.svg   # imported -> processed and renamed
├── vite.config.ts
└── package.json
    "scripts": {
      "dev": "vite",
      "build": "tsc -b && vite build",   // tsc checks types, then Vite builds
      "preview": "vite preview"
    }
takeaways: index.html at the project's top level is the entry point
Files in src/ are processed; files in public/ are copied unchanged
dev runs on port 5173, preview on 4173
Vite removes TypeScript types but never checks them; tsc does
pitfalls: Importing a file from public/: it skips processing, and its path can break once the app is served from a sub-folder.

quiz.q: Where should a file live if it must be served at exactly `/robots.txt`, unprocessed?
quiz.explain: Files in public/ are copied to the top of the output as they are, without renaming or converting.

quiz.q: Your TypeScript code has a type mistake. What does `vite build` on its own do?
options: Builds anyway, because Vite only removes types
quiz.explain: Vite strips types without checking them; run `tsc` first if you want mistakes to stop the build.

concepts.name: Importing CSS and static assets
concepts.summary: Import CSS files, scoped CSS modules, images and text straight from JavaScript, and change what an import gives you with ?raw or ?url.
concepts.why: In Vite, styles and images are part of the module graph just like code, which changes how you refer to them.
concepts.body: In a plain HTML page you add styles and images with `` and `` tags. In a Vite project you usually **import** them from JavaScript instead, just like code, and Vite works out the rest. **CSS**: - `import "./style.css"` adds the styles to the page. In the dev server, edits show instantly; in the build, the styles are pulled out into their own `.css` file. - A file named `*.module.css` is a **CSS module**: `import styles from "./card.module.css"` gives an object whose properties are class names made unique to that file, like `_card_1x2y3`. Two files can both use a `.card` class without clashing. Many teams write styles in **Sass** or Less: extended versions of CSS with extras such as variables, which must be converted to plain CSS. Vite does that once you install the converter (`npm i -D sass-embedded`); no settings needed. In the build, Vite also minifies your CSS and rewrites newer CSS features so older browsers understand them. **Images and other files**: `import logoUrl from "./logo.svg"` gives you a string, the URL to put in an ``. In the build, the file is copied with a fingerprint of its contents in its name (`logo-Bx3k9.svg`), so a changed image gets a new name and browsers never show a stale copy. Very small files, under 4 KB (about 4,000 bytes), aren't copied at all. Their contents are written straight into a **data URI**: a URL that starts with `data:` and holds the file itself. That saves the browser one download. Add a suffix after `?` to change what an import gives you: - `?url`: always a URL to a separate file. - `?raw`: the file's contents as a string. - `?inline`: always a data URI. - `?worker`: a **Web Worker**, a script that runs alongside your page without freezing it, for heavy calculations. `import data from "./data.json"` gives you the parsed JSON, and you can import single top-level properties by name: `import { version } from "../package.json"`. Image paths inside CSS (`url(./bg.png)`) and in `index.html` are handled the same way as imports. When you need a file's URL without importing it, `new URL("./img.png", import.meta.url)` works too: `import.meta.url` is the current module's own address, so the path is read relative to this file.
takeaways: Import CSS from JavaScript; `*.module.css` gives class names unique to that file
Imported files become fingerprinted URLs, or data URIs if tiny
Suffixes change the result: `?url`, `?raw`, `?inline`, `?worker`
Sass or Less works once its package is installed
pitfalls: Building a file path from pieces of text while the app runs (`"./img/" + name`): Vite can't see it in advance, so the file isn't copied or renamed.

quiz.q: What does `import text from './notes.txt?raw'` give you?
options: The file's contents as a string
quiz.explain: `?raw` imports the file's contents as a string.

concepts.name: Environment variables and modes
concepts.summary: Read VITE_ variables through import.meta.env, load different .env files per mode, and keep secrets out of the code sent to browsers.
concepts.why: Every app needs settings that differ between your laptop and the live site, and leaking a secret into browser code is a classic mistake.
concepts.body:
You know environment variables and `.env` files from Node. Code running in a browser has no `process.env`, so Vite gives you `import.meta.env` instead. (`import.meta` is an object every ES module gets, holding information about that module.)

What `import.meta.env` contains:

- Built-in values: `MODE` (see below), `DEV` and `PROD` (true or false), and `BASE_URL` (the path the app is served from, usually `/`).
- Your own variables, **but only those whose names start with `VITE_`**, such as `VITE_API_URL`. Others, like `DB_PASSWORD`, stay hidden on purpose.

Vite reads `.env` files from the project folder in this order, later ones winning:

- `.env`, then `.env.local` (always loaded; `.local` files are kept out of version control)
- `.env.[mode]`, then `.env.[mode].local`

A variable set in the terminal beats them all: `VITE_API_URL=... vite build`.

A **mode** is a name for a setup, such as development, staging (a test copy of the live site) or production. `vite` uses `development` and `vite build` uses `production`; `--mode staging` picks another one and loads `.env.staging`. Mode is separate from `NODE_ENV`.

The key fact: Vite **pastes each value into your JavaScript, as text, when it builds**. The finished files contain `"https://api.example.com"` where your code said `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`. Three consequences:

- Never put secrets in `VITE_` variables. Anyone can open the downloaded files and read them.
- Values are always strings: compare with `"true"`, or convert `"3"` with `Number()`.
- Changing a value needs a new build. For settings that must change without rebuilding, have the app download a `config.json` when it starts.

Inside `vite.config.ts` itself, `.env` files are not loaded for you; call `loadEnv(mode, process.cwd())` if your settings need them.
concepts.code:
# .env
VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com
DB_PASSWORD=hunter2            # NOT visible to app code: no VITE_ prefix

# .env.staging
VITE_API_URL=https://staging-api.example.com

// src/api.js
console.log(import.meta.env.MODE);          // "development" | "production" | "staging"
console.log(import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL);  // pasted in at build time
console.log(import.meta.env.DB_PASSWORD);   // undefined
const debug = import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG === "true"; // values are strings

# build for staging
npx vite build --mode staging
takeaways: Only `VITE_`-prefixed variables reach browser code
`.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.[mode]`, `.env.[mode].local`; the terminal wins
Values are pasted in at build time, as strings
Never put secrets in VITE_ variables
pitfalls: Putting a payment service's secret key in VITE_STRIPE_SECRET, which ships it to every visitor's browser.

quiz.q: Why doesn't changing a `VITE_` variable on the server affect a site that's already built?
options: Vite stores it in the browser
Its value was pasted into the JavaScript files at build time
quiz.explain: Vite replaces import.meta.env.VITE_* with the actual values during the build, so only a new build changes them.

concepts.name: Configuration and the dev server
concepts.summary: Write vite.config with defineConfig, add import shortcuts, and set the dev server's port and a proxy that forwards calls to your backend.
concepts.why: Most real projects need short import paths and a way to reach their backend while developing.
concepts.body:
Vite's settings live in `vite.config.ts` (or `.js`). The file exports an object, ideally wrapped in `defineConfig(...)` so your editor can suggest option names. It can also export a function that receives `{ command, mode }`: `command` is `"serve"` for the dev server and `"build"` for builds, so settings can differ between them.

**Plugins** are add-ons that teach Vite new things, and the `plugins` list is where they go. The most common adds support for a UI library (UI, short for user interface, is what people see and click on): `react()` from `@vitejs/plugin-react` lets Vite understand React code. Plugins get their own lesson later.

**Import shortcuts**: `resolve.alias` can map `@` to the `src/` folder, so `import Button from "@/components/Button"` works from any folder instead of `../../../components/Button`. TypeScript must know too: add the same mapping under `paths` in `tsconfig.json`, TypeScript's settings file (or set Vite's `resolve.tsconfigPaths: true` to read it from there).

**Sub-path**: `base` is the path the app is served from. If it will live at `example.com/docs/`, set `base: "/docs/"` so every file link includes it.

**Dev server**: `server.port` changes 5173; `server.strictPort: true` fails instead of moving to the next free port; `server.open` opens a browser; `server.host: true` lets other devices on your network reach it. If you reach the dev server through a name other than localhost, such as a tunnel service that gives your laptop a public web address, list that name in `server.allowedHosts`.

**Proxy**: your app's **backend**, the server program that holds data and answers your app's `fetch` calls, often runs separately, say on port 8000. Calling it straight from a page on port 5173 runs into the browser's CORS rule, because a different port counts as a different site. `server.proxy` fixes this: the dev server accepts calls such as `/api/users` itself and passes them on to the backend, so the browser only ever talks to one address. A server that passes requests along like this is a **proxy**.

Proxy options: `changeOrigin: true` makes the forwarded request look as if it had been sent to the backend directly; `rewrite` can strip the `/api` prefix; `ws: true` also forwards **WebSockets**, connections that stay open so the server can push live updates.

Vite restarts the dev server by itself when `vite.config.ts` changes. The dev server is built for your own computer, without protection against attacks, so never make it reachable from the internet as if it were a real server.
takeaways: `defineConfig` gives editor help; the function form sees command and mode
An `@` alias needs the same mapping in tsconfig.json
`server.proxy` forwards calls to your backend, avoiding CORS errors in development
Set `base` when the app is served from a sub-path
pitfalls: Opening the dev server to the internet as if it were a real server.

quiz.q: What does a `server.proxy` entry for `/api` solve during development?
options: Calling the backend through the dev server's own address, avoiding CORS errors
quiz.explain: The dev server passes matching requests on to the backend, so the browser only sees one address.

concepts.name: Hot module replacement
concepts.summary: See how HMR swaps changed modules into the open page, what an HMR boundary is, and how import.meta.hot lets a module update itself.
concepts.why: Knowing when HMR applies and when the page fully reloads explains lost state and stale code while developing.
concepts.body:
Hot module replacement (HMR) updates the open page when you save a file. Here is how. Vite watches your files. When one changes, it finds that module in the module graph and asks: does this module, or a module that imports it, or one that imports that, know how to accept a new version of itself? The first one that does is an **HMR boundary**.

Vite then sends a message to the page over a WebSocket that the dev server keeps open. Vite's small helper script in the page downloads the new versions of the changed modules and swaps them in. Nothing else reloads.

Most of the time you don't write boundaries yourself:

- UI-library plugins make each component a boundary. (A component is one reusable piece of a page, like a button or a menu.) React's version is **Fast Refresh**, in `@vitejs/plugin-react`; Vue, Svelte and Solid have their own. They keep what's on screen, such as typed text or an open menu, across edits.
- CSS changes are swapped in place.
- If Vite climbs all the way to the entry without finding a boundary, it **reloads the whole page**, and anything the page was holding is lost.

Plain modules can opt in with **`import.meta.hot`**:

- `accept(cb)`: this module accepts updates; `cb` receives the new version.
- `dispose(cb)`: undo what the old version started (timers, event handlers) before it is replaced.
- `data`: an object that survives from one version to the next, for keeping values.
- `invalidate()`: give up and let the importers deal with the update.

Always wrap this code in `if (import.meta.hot)`. In a production build `import.meta.hot` is undefined, and Vite removes the whole block.

Gotchas: Fast Refresh only works when a file exports nothing but components; export a constant from the same file and every edit reloads the page. A module that adds an event handler to the whole page needs `dispose`, or each edit adds one more. If your files live inside Docker (a tool that runs apps in sealed-off containers) or WSL (Linux running inside Windows), Vite may not notice changes; set `server.watch.usePolling: true` so it checks the files regularly.
takeaways: HMR climbs the importers to the nearest module that accepts updates
No boundary found means a full page reload
`accept`, `dispose`, `data`, `invalidate` on import.meta.hot
Wrap it in `if (import.meta.hot)`; it's removed from production builds
pitfalls: Exporting constants and components from the same React file, which turns every edit into a full reload.

quiz.q: A changed module and all its importers up to the entry have no HMR boundary. What happens?
quiz.explain: With no module willing to accept the update, Vite falls back to reloading the page.

concepts.name: Production builds and deployment
concepts.summary: Build with vite build, understand fingerprinted files and code splitting, choose which browsers to support, and put dist/ online.
concepts.why: The build output is what your users actually download.
concepts.body:
`vite build` writes everything users need into `dist/`: the rewritten `index.html`, and an `assets/` folder of JavaScript, CSS and images. Each asset's name contains a **content hash**, a short code computed from the file's contents (`index-D0ftifMV.js`). Change one character and the code changes; leave the file alone and it stays the same.

That makes caching easy. Browsers can keep `assets/` files for a year, because a changed file always arrives under a new name. Only `index.html`, which points to the current names, must never be kept: users should get a fresh copy on every visit.

What happens during the build:

- **Bundling** with Rolldown, including **tree-shaking**: exports nothing imports are left out, like shaking a tree so the dead leaves fall.
- **Code splitting**: each dynamic `import()` becomes a separate file, a **chunk**, downloaded only when that code is needed. Code that several chunks use goes into a shared chunk.
- **Minifying** JavaScript and CSS; each chunk gets its own CSS file.

**Which browsers**: `build.target` decides how new the output may be. The default, `'baseline-widely-available'`, means features every major browser has supported for about two and a half years; newer syntax in your code is rewritten into older equivalents. Vite does **not** add **polyfills**, extra code that recreates a missing built-in feature in old browsers. For very old browsers, add `@vitejs/plugin-legacy`.

**Source maps**: `build.sourcemap: true` writes `.map` files that connect the minified code to your original files, so error messages point at your real line numbers. `'hidden'` writes them but leaves out the note in the code that tells browsers where they are, so you can upload them to an error-reporting service without showing your original code to visitors.

Other options: `build.outDir`, `build.assetsInlineLimit` (the 4 KB data URI limit) and `build.chunkSizeWarningLimit` (the "chunk larger than 500 kB" warning).

**Deploying**: `dist/` is just files, so any **static host**, a service that serves files exactly as they are, can serve it: Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages, GitHub Pages or your own Nginx. If your app switches pages itself with JavaScript, without asking the server (as React Router and similar libraries do), set the hosting service to answer unknown paths like `/settings` with `index.html`. If the app lives under a sub-path, set `base`.
takeaways: Output is plain files: content-hashed assets plus index.html
Each dynamic `import()` becomes a chunk downloaded on demand
Default target is baseline-widely-available; no automatic polyfills
Cache assets for a year; never cache index.html
pitfalls: Letting browsers keep index.html for a long time, so after a deploy they keep asking for old file names.

quiz.q: Why can files in dist/assets be cached for a year?
options: Their names contain content hashes, so changed content gets a new URL
quiz.explain: With content hashing, every changed file gets a new URL, so a file at an old URL never changes.

concepts.name: Using plugins and framework integrations
concepts.summary: Add official and community plugins, control their order and when they run, and see why many Rollup plugins work in Vite too.
concepts.why: Support for UI libraries, old browsers, installable apps and much more comes from plugins.
concepts.body:
Out of the box, Vite understands JavaScript, TypeScript, CSS, JSON and asset files. Everything else comes from a plugin in the `plugins` list.

- Official plugins: `@vitejs/plugin-react` (React's **JSX**, HTML-like tags inside JavaScript, plus Fast Refresh), `@vitejs/plugin-react-swc` (the same, using a faster converter called SWC), `@vitejs/plugin-vue`, `@vitejs/plugin-vue-jsx` and `@vitejs/plugin-legacy` (old browsers). Svelte, Solid, Preact and Qwik publish their own.
- Community plugins add apps that users can install and use offline (PWAs), SVG images imported as components, image compression, charts of bundle size and much more.

**Rollup** is the bundler Vite used for builds before version 8, and its plugin format became a standard. A Vite plugin is a Rollup plugin with extra Vite-only parts, so many Rollup (and Rolldown) plugins work unchanged. The extras plug into the dev server and into `index.html`.

Controlling plugins:

- `enforce: "pre"` or `"post"` runs a plugin before or after Vite's own built-in plugins. A plugin that must see your code before anything converts it uses `pre`.
- `apply: "serve"` or `"build"` (or a function) limits a plugin to the dev server or to builds.
- Nested lists are flattened, and `false` or `null` entries are skipped, so `mode === "analyze" && visualizer()` adds a plugin only in that mode.

Many **frameworks**, larger toolkits that also decide how your app's pages, files and data loading are organized, are themselves Vite plugins plus conventions: Nuxt, SvelteKit, Astro, React Router (framework mode), TanStack Start and Vike. They usually set Vite up for you, so read their docs before adding plugins by hand.

Keep the list short: plugins can run on every file Vite converts, and slow plugins are a common reason for a slow dev server.
takeaways: Plugins add UI libraries and features; Vite plugins extend Rollup's format
`enforce` orders plugins, `apply` limits them to dev or build
`false` entries in `plugins` are skipped
Frameworks like Nuxt and SvelteKit are Vite plugins plus conventions
pitfalls: Stacking many heavy plugins and then blaming Vite for slow file conversion.

quiz.q: How do you make a plugin run only for `vite build`?
options: Put it last in the list
quiz.explain: `apply` limits a plugin to the serve or the build command.

concepts.name: Dependency pre-bundling
concepts.summary: Understand why Vite pre-bundles packages from node_modules, how the saved result is reused, and fix problems with optimizeDeps include and exclude.
concepts.why: Most 'works after a restart' and 'two copies of React' problems in development trace back to pre-bundling.
concepts.body:
Vite's dev server pre-bundles your npm packages. Here is the detail. On the first start, Vite scans your code for **bare imports**: imports of a package by name rather than by file path, such as `import { debounce } from "lodash-es"`. It bundles each of those packages (with Rolldown) into `node_modules/.vite/deps`, for two reasons:

- **Converting to ES modules**: many packages still ship CommonJS, or **UMD** (an old format meant to work everywhere), which browsers can't `import`.
- **Fewer requests**: a package built from hundreds of small modules becomes one file. Otherwise the browser would discover them one level at a time (import, wait, import, wait), a slow chain called a **request waterfall**.

The browser is told to keep these files for a year, and Vite rewrites your imports to point at them.

Vite throws the saved result away and rebuilds it when your lock file, the relevant settings or `patchedDependencies` (fixes you've applied to installed packages) change. To force a rebuild, run `vite --force` or delete `node_modules/.vite`.

When things go wrong:

- **A package found late**: an import that only shows up after you navigate, say in a page that loads only when visited, makes Vite pre-bundle again and reload the page. Add the package to `optimizeDeps.include` so it's done at start-up.
- **Linked packages** in a **monorepo** (one repository holding several of your own packages) count as your own code and aren't pre-bundled. If one ships CommonJS, add it to `include`.
- **Large packages that already ship browser-ready ES modules** can go in `optimizeDeps.exclude`.
- **Two copies of a package that must exist only once**, such as React, which breaks when two copies run: add `resolve.dedupe: ["react", "react-dom"]`.

Pre-bundling only happens in the dev server; production builds bundle packages together with your code.
takeaways: Pre-bundling converts CommonJS to ES modules and collapses many files into one
The result lives in node_modules/.vite; `--force` rebuilds it
`include` late-found or linked CommonJS packages; `exclude` browser-ready ones
Use `resolve.dedupe` for packages that must exist once, like React
pitfalls: Repeatedly deleting node_modules instead of adding a late-found package to `optimizeDeps.include`.

quiz.q: Opening a page that loads on visit causes 'new dependencies optimized, reloading'. What is the fix?
quiz.explain: Listing it up front lets Vite pre-bundle it at start-up instead of halfway through your session.

concepts.name: Library mode
concepts.summary: Build a publishable npm package with build.lib: entry files, output formats, file names and dependencies left out, plus types and exports.
concepts.why: Shared component libraries and packages for other developers need different output than an app.
concepts.body:
An app build produces `index.html` and fingerprinted files. A **library**, code other projects install from npm, needs something else: fixed file names, ES module output (and sometimes CommonJS), and none of its own dependencies copied inside. Vite's **library mode** does this:

- `build.lib.entry`: the library's entry point file (or an object listing several).
- `build.lib.formats`: defaults to `['es', 'umd']` for one entry; `['es', 'cjs']` is usual for npm. The `umd` and `iife` formats (both can run straight from a `<script>` tag) also need `name`: the global variable the library is placed in, like `window.MyLib`.
- `build.lib.fileName`: the base name of the output files.
- `build.rolldownOptions.external`: packages to **leave out**, so the project that installs your library uses its own copy. List your dependencies and peer dependencies here, such as `react` and `react/jsx-runtime`. Forget this and you ship a second copy of React inside your package.

What Vite won't do for you:

- **Type declarations**: `.d.ts` files that describe your library's types for TypeScript users. Run `tsc --emitDeclarationOnly` or a plugin such as `vite-plugin-dts`.
- **package.json**: point `exports` (with `types`, `import` and `require` conditions) at the built files, and list `dist` in `files`.
- **CSS** comes out as a separate file that users of your library must import; say so in your README.

For a library of plain TypeScript, with no CSS and no UI-library code, tools made for the job (tsdown, built on Rolldown, or plain `tsc`) are often simpler. Library mode shines for component libraries that need Vite's CSS handling and UI-library plugins.
takeaways: `build.lib` sets entry, formats and file names
Leave dependencies and peer dependencies out with `external`
Generate .d.ts files separately; set up `exports` and `files` yourself
Consider tsdown or tsc for plain TypeScript libraries
pitfalls: Forgetting to leave React out of a component library, shipping a second copy of React.

quiz.q: Why mark `react` as external in a React component library build?
options: So the app's own single copy of React is used instead of a bundled one
quiz.explain: A bundled copy would be a second React running beside the app's own, and React breaks when two copies run together.

concepts.name: Writing Vite plugins
concepts.summary: Write resolveId, load and transform hooks, create virtual modules, and use Vite-only hooks like configureServer and transformIndexHtml.
concepts.why: Custom plugins handle code generation, integrations and build-time changes that no setting covers.
concepts.body:
A plugin is an object with a `name` and **hook** functions: functions Vite calls at set moments, such as "an import needs looking up" or "a file was loaded". Plugins are usually returned from a function so they can take options.

**Rollup-compatible hooks** (run in dev and build):

- `resolveId(source, importer)`: turn an import string into an **id**, usually a file path. Returning an id that starts with `\0` (an invisible null character) marks a **virtual module**: one that a plugin makes up rather than reads from a file, so other plugins and file reading leave it alone.
- `load(id)`: return the code for an id, for instance generated code for a virtual module.
- `transform(code, id)`: change a module's code. Return `{ code, map }`, where `map` is a source map, whenever you can.
- `buildStart`, `generateBundle` and other build-stage hooks.

Rolldown is written in Rust and runs as fast native code, so every call into a JavaScript hook costs time. **Hook filters** let it skip that call for files you don't care about: `transform: { filter: { id: /\.md$/ }, handler }` runs `handler` only for `.md` files. The `/\.md$/` part is a **regular expression**, a pattern for matching text; this one means "ends in .md".

**Vite-only hooks**:

- `config` / `configResolved`: change, or read, the final settings.
- `configureServer(server)`: add **middleware** to the dev server, functions that see each incoming request and either answer it or pass it on, with `server.middlewares.use`; or watch extra files.
- `transformIndexHtml`: add tags to `index.html`.
- `hotUpdate`: customize HMR for certain files.

By convention, virtual modules are imported with a `virtual:` prefix (`import info from "virtual:build-info"`). Name plugins `vite-plugin-*`, or `rolldown-plugin-*` if they work with any Rolldown setup. To see what each plugin did to a file, use `vite-plugin-inspect`, which shows every step per module.
takeaways: resolveId + load create virtual modules (`\0` prefix)
transform rewrites code; return a source map with it
Hook filters let Rolldown skip JavaScript calls for files you don't handle
Vite-only hooks: configureServer, transformIndexHtml, hotUpdate
pitfalls: Checking every file name with a regular expression inside the hook instead of using a hook filter.

quiz.q: Why do virtual module ids returned from resolveId start with `\0`?
options: It tells other plugins and file reading that this is not a real file
quiz.explain: The null-character prefix is the Rollup convention for ids that other plugins should leave alone.

concepts.name: SSR and the Environment API
concepts.summary: Build pages on the server with Vite in middleware mode, make separate browser and server builds, and understand environments and module runners.
concepts.why: Frameworks that build pages on the server sit on these features, and fixing their problems means understanding them.
concepts.body:
Normally the browser receives a nearly empty `index.html`, and JavaScript then builds the page. With **server-side rendering (SSR)**, the server runs your app code first and sends finished HTML, so the page appears sooner and search engines can read it. That means Node must run code written for Vite (JSX, TypeScript, CSS imports), which plain Node can't. Vite helps in two phases.

**Development**: create the Vite dev server in **middleware mode** and plug it into your own Node server (Express, Hono and similar). For each request, load your server entry file through Vite, which converts it on the fly and supports HMR; produce the HTML; then pass it through `vite.transformIndexHtml` so the browser scripts and Vite's HMR helper get added. The classic call is `vite.ssrLoadModule(url)`.

**Production**: build twice, `vite build` for the browser and `vite build --ssr src/entry-server.js` for the server, and have your server import the built server file directly, with no Vite running. `ssr.noExternal` lists packages to bundle into the server build; by default, packages in node_modules are left for Node to load.

The **Environment API** (new in Vite 6 and still evolving) generalizes this. One Vite server or build now has several named **environments**, by default `client` (the browser) and `ssr` (the server). Each has its own module graph, its own rules for picking a package's files, and its own chain of plugin steps.

You can add custom environments for other places code runs, such as edge servers: machines spread around the world that run small pieces of JavaScript close to users. Code runs inside an environment through a **module runner**, which can live in the same Node process or in a different JavaScript runtime such as workerd (Cloudflare's) or Deno. Frameworks use this so that, during development, server code already runs in the same kind of runtime it will use in production.

App authors rarely use these APIs directly; they arrive through frameworks. Plugin authors must keep environments in mind: inside a hook, `this.environment` says which one is running.
takeaways: Dev SSR: Vite in middleware mode runs server code with HMR
Prod SSR: separate browser and --ssr builds, no Vite at runtime
Environments: client, ssr and custom ones, each with its own module graph
Module runners run an environment's code, possibly in another runtime
pitfalls: Shipping the development middleware setup to production instead of the built server file.

quiz.q: What does the Environment API add over the classic SSR setup?
options: Several named environments, each with its own module graph and runtime
quiz.explain: It turns the fixed browser/server pair into configurable environments, run through module runners.

concepts.name: Rolldown, chunking and performance
concepts.summary: Know what changed with Rolldown and Oxc in Vite 8, group code into chunks yourself, and find out why a dev server is slow or a bundle is big.
concepts.why: Large apps run into slow first starts and oversized downloads, and fixing them takes knowing the toolchain.
concepts.body:
Before version 8, Vite used two tools: **esbuild** for converting files and pre-bundling, and **Rollup** for production builds. The two didn't always behave the same. **Vite 8** replaced both with Rolldown (the bundler) and **Oxc** (which reads, converts and minifies code), both written by the VoidZero team in Rust, a language that compiles to fast native code. One toolchain for dev and build means more consistent results and much faster builds.

Settings moved with it: `build.rolldownOptions` replaces `build.rollupOptions` (the old name still works but is **deprecated**: kept for now, due to be removed), and the `oxc` option replaces `esbuild`.

**Chunks**: by default Rolldown makes one chunk per entry and per dynamic import, plus shared chunks. To group modules yourself, use `output.codeSplitting.groups`. Each group has a `name` and a `test` (a regular expression or function that picks module paths), plus optional `minSize`, `maxSize` and `priority`. Rollup's older `manualChunks` function still works but is deprecated.

Why group? Your own code changes with every deploy, but packages like React rarely do. Put them in a separate `vendor` chunk and its content hash stays the same, so returning visitors' browsers can reuse their saved copy. Split too finely, though, and the page has to make dozens of small requests, some waiting on others.

**A slow dev server**:

- Find slow plugins with `vite --debug plugin-transform` or `vite-plugin-inspect`.
- Avoid **barrel files**: an `index.ts` that only re-exports hundreds of modules. Importing one thing from it makes the dev server load them all.
- Write file extensions in imports (`./Button.tsx`) so Vite has less guessing to do, and list often-used files in `server.warmup.clientFiles` so they're converted before the browser asks.

**A big bundle**: chart it with `rollup-plugin-visualizer` or `vite-bundle-analyzer`. Then swap heavy packages for lighter ones, load rarely visited pages only when they're visited, and check that tree-shaking works; packages that declare `"sideEffects": false` in package.json let the bundler drop their unused files safely.
takeaways: Vite 8: Rolldown + Oxc; `rolldownOptions` and `oxc` replace `rollupOptions` and `esbuild`
`codeSplitting.groups` controls chunks; `manualChunks` is deprecated
Barrel files and slow plugins are the usual dev-server slowdowns
Measure the bundle before optimizing it
pitfalls: Splitting every package into its own chunk, creating dozens of small requests.

quiz.explain: Vite 8 bundles with Rolldown; rollupOptions remains only as a deprecated alternative name.
